newsitem.title: USA: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS / Intel LEAPS and FOMC.
newsitem.headline: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS / Intel LEAPS and FOMC.

text.p: Intel Corp LEAPS, both puts and calls, saw some big trades, which were seen to be an interest-rate play ahead of Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee meeting, traders said.
Intel LEAPS (long-term equity anticipation securities) with an at-the-money strike price of 130 and expiration in January 1998 were the heaviest traded puts and calls on the American Stock Exchange.
The 130 puts had turnover of more than 5,700 contracts by late trade, and calls had more than 5,300. Of that volume, 5,000 each were traded in combination, traders said.
"Those 5,000 in puts and calls were apparently done as a forward conversion," said Andrew Schwarz, senior partner of AGS Specialist Partners.
"I think it's an interest-rate speculation...but it could be a lot of other things, none of which anybody in the trading crowd (on AMEX floor) was sure of," he added.

A forward conversion involves a long stock, long put and short call position. The long put and short call positions essentially make a synthetic short position on the stock with a short-term interest rate priced in.
The calls in question changed hands at 18-1/4 and the puts at 16, making the LEAPS deal a 2-1/4 point credit trade.

The deal could have been aimed at capturing an overshooting in the interest rate markets prior to the FOMC meeting, at which the Federal Reserve was widely expected to raise interest rates by 25 basis points, trader said.
But it was difficult to tell how interest rates worked out in the deal because it was unclear what the expected dividend was or how the stock purchase was financed or margined, traders said.
With just under 10 months to expiration and the stock roughly at 130, the credit itself was equal to an annualized interest rate of about two percent.
One brokerage firm trader said the deal could be viewed as a downward-biased directional and volatility play, given the steadily declining stock price.
"If you are long the stock and expect it to fall further, it's a cheaper way of buying a put," he said.
Intel shares have been gradually eroding since topping out at 165 at the start of February, drawing a clearly defined declining channel on the daily chart.
The trader added that implied volatilities tend to rise when the stock falls and decline when the stock rises, working in favor of the LEAPS position.
Harrison Roth, first vice president of Cowen & Co, said implied volatilities for Intel options and LEAPS had become plump in recent weeks. The LEAPS stood at about 40 percent.
Michael Schwartz, a managing director of Oppenheimer & Co, said a Fed tightening on Tuesday would probably have a positive effect on the stock market in general.
"If they don't raise rates, we can probably be set back even further," Schwartz said.
